Apocrypha
uh-POK-rih-fuh
n.
From Greek apokryphos, “hidden, concealed,” from apo (away) + kryptein (to hide). The term came to denote books of doubtful authority, outside the recognized canon.

See also: Apocrypha

📖 Biblical Definition

The Apocrypha (the “hidden” or doubtful books) are a collection of Jewish writings—such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees—composed largely in the intertestamental period, found in the Greek Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate but absent from the Hebrew canon of the Old Testament. The question they raise is one of canonicity: are they part of God’s inspired Word? The Protestant churches answer that they are not. The Hebrew canon received by the Jews, to whom were committed the oracles of God, never included them; the Lord Jesus and the apostles, who quoted the Old Testament constantly, never cited them as Scripture; they were not written in Hebrew as the recognized prophetic books were; and they contain historical errors and doctrines (such as prayers for the dead and salvation by almsgiving) at variance with the rest of Scripture. The Westminster Confession declares plainly that the books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of Scripture, and therefore are of no authority in the church of God, nor to be otherwise approved or made use of than other human writings. The Roman communion, by contrast, at the Council of Trent in 1546 declared most of these books canonical (terming them deuterocanonical), partly in response to the Reformation’s appeal to Scripture. Protestants may read the Apocrypha as useful for history and edification, but never as the inspired and authoritative Word of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines APOCRYPHA as books whose authority is doubtful, and which are not admitted into the sacred canon by Protestants.

expand to see more

APOCRYPHA, n. — Books whose authors are not known, and whose authenticity, as inspired writings, is not admitted, and which are therefore not considered a part of the sacred canon of the Scripture. When the Jews ceased to consider their writings as inspired... such books were called apocryphal.

APOCRYPHAL, a. — Pertaining to the Apocrypha; not canonical; of uncertain authority or credit; false; fictitious.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The corruption is the elevation of the Apocrypha to canonical status, decreed by Rome at Trent (1546) to buttress doctrines like purgatory and prayers for the dead that Scripture proper does not teach.

expand to see more

The decisive corruption surrounding the Apocrypha is its elevation to the status of inspired Scripture. For centuries these books circulated in the Greek and Latin Bibles in a recognized second rank—useful, edifying, even read in churches, but distinguished from the canonical Scriptures and not used to establish doctrine. Jerome himself, who translated the Vulgate, sharply distinguished them from the canon. But at the Council of Trent in 1546, in direct reaction to the Reformation’s appeal to Scripture alone, Rome declared most of the Apocrypha to be canonical and bound the faithful to receive them as sacred—not least because texts like Second Maccabees were enlisted to support prayers for the dead and the doctrine of purgatory.

This was a corruption on two counts. First, it added to the canon books that the Jewish people, the custodians of the Old Testament oracles, never received, that Christ and the apostles never cited as Scripture, and that bear marks of error inconsistent with inspiration. Second, it did so to prop up doctrines that the undisputed Scriptures do not teach, thus using a disputed authority to license unbiblical practice. The Protestant position is neither contempt nor canonization: the Apocrypha may be read with profit as ancient Jewish literature and a window on the intertestamental age, but it is no part of the God-breathed canon and carries no authority to bind the conscience or to establish any article of faith.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name apokryphos (hidden, doubtful) marks these as books outside the kanōn (canon, measuring rule), distinguished from the Hebrew oracles entrusted to Israel.
